events.title: Plato, Phaedrus
events.description: In this dialogue Socrates and the young Phaedrus walk outside the walls of Athens and discuss love, rhetoric, and the soul. It closes with the myth of Theuth and Thamus, a critique of writing as a text that cannot answer back when it is questioned.
events.uncertain: The date of composition is inferred from the dialogue's style and its place among Plato's works. Estimates range from about 370 to 360 BCE.

events.title: Confucius (attributed), Analects
events.who: Disciples and later followers of Confucius
events.description: The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges between Confucius and his disciples, assembled after his death. Its question-and-answer form makes ethical teaching an act of conversation between teacher and student.
events.quote: Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application?
events.uncertain: The text was compiled in stages, and scholars dispute when it was put together. The year 400 BCE is only a placement on the axis. Legge's wording should be checked against the 1861 edition.

events.title: Mary Shelley, Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus
events.description: Victor Frankenstein, a young natural philosopher, assembles a living being and then abandons it. The creature learns language and argues its case to its maker, and the story is framed by a chain of letters and nested narrations.
events.quote: It was on a dreary night of November that I beheld the accomplishment of my toils.
events.quote_attribution: Frankenstein, vol. I, ch. 4 (1818); ch. 5 in the 1831 edition
events.uncertain: The revised 1831 edition differs substantially from the 1818 text, so the class should state which edition it reads. The January 1 publication date is the one usually given.

events.title: Oscar Wilde, The Picture of Dorian Gray
events.description: The novel first appeared in a magazine in thirteen chapters. Wilde then expanded and revised it into a book with a preface in 1891. A young man's portrait ages and records his corruption while he himself stays unchanged, a story about art, influence, and the self as a made surface.
events.quote_attribution: The Picture of Dorian Gray, Preface (1891 book edition)
events.uncertain: The July 1890 issue was released around June 20, 1890. The quoted preface belongs to the 1891 edition and first appeared in the Fortnightly Review in March 1891, so it is not in the 1890 magazine text.

events.title: Oscar Wilde, The Critic as Artist
events.date_display: July and September 1890 (The Nineteenth Century); revised in Intentions, 1891
events.description: This is a two-part dialogue between Gilbert and Ernest that argues criticism is itself a creative art. It first appeared in a magazine as The True Function and Value of Criticism, and Wilde revised it under its present title for the essay collection Intentions.
events.quote: The one duty we owe to history is to rewrite it.
events.quote_attribution: The Critic as Artist, Part I, in Intentions (1891)
events.uncertain: The date given here is the first magazine publication under the earlier title. Intentions was published in May 1891, and the wording of the quote should be checked against the 1891 text.

events.title: Henri Bergson, Laughter (Le Rire)
events.date_display: 1900 (book; serialized in the Revue de Paris, 1899)
events.description: Bergson's essay on the comic argues that we laugh when a living person behaves like a mechanism. His idea of rigidity and automatism set against the suppleness of life is a useful lens on robots and scripted speech.
events.quote: something mechanical encrusted upon the living
events.quote_attribution: Laughter, ch. I, sec. V, trans. Cloudesley Brereton and Fred Rothwell (1911)
events.uncertain: The section number of the quote should be checked against the 1911 translation.

events.title: Karel Čapek, R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots)
events.description: In this Czech play a factory mass-produces artificial workers who eventually rise up against humanity. It introduced the word robot, which Čapek's brother Josef suggested, into world languages.
events.uncertain: Some sources report an amateur performance in Hradec Králové in early January 1921, before the Prague premiere. The play was published in 1920. The English translation by Paul Selver dates from 1923.

events.title: James Whale (director), Frankenstein
events.description: Universal's film was adapted from Peggy Webling's stage play rather than directly from Shelley's novel, and it starred Boris Karloff as the creature. It established the popular image of the monster as a near-mute figure, a sharp contrast with the eloquent creature of the novel.
events.uncertain: US works first published in 1931 enter the public domain on January 1, 2027, so the film is still in copyright in 2026. The premiere date should be checked against the general release date.

events.title: Sacks, Schegloff, and Jefferson, A Simplest Systematics for the Organization of Turn-Taking for Conversation
events.who: Harvey Sacks, Emanuel A. Schegloff, Gail Jefferson
events.description: This founding paper of conversation analysis models how speakers allocate turns locally, moment by moment. The model rests on recordings of naturally occurring talk and explains why speakers mostly avoid both gaps and overlaps.
events.uncertain: The month comes from the issue number, and the page range is usually given as 696–735.

events.title: H. P. Grice, Logic and Conversation
events.date_display: 1975 (Syntax and Semantics 3: Speech Acts); delivered as William James Lectures, 1967
events.description: Grice proposes the Cooperative Principle and its maxims of quantity, quality, relation, and manner. He uses them to explain conversational implicature, the gap between what a speaker says and what the speaker means.
events.uncertain: The lectures were delivered at Harvard in 1967, and the essay was published in 1975 in a volume edited by Peter Cole and Jerry Morgan.

events.title: Askell et al., A General Language Assistant as a Laboratory for Alignment
events.description: The Anthropic paper frames the goal of a helpful, honest, and harmless text assistant. It studies prompting, preference modeling, and related baselines as ways of shaping a language model into that role.
events.uncertain: The paper was later revised on arXiv.

events.title: Shanahan, McDonell, and Reynolds, Role Play with Large Language Models
events.who: Murray Shanahan, Kyle McDonell, Laria Reynolds
events.description: The authors argue that a dialogue agent is best understood as playing a role, or as maintaining a set of possible characters. On this view the model is not a being with beliefs of its own. They use the framing to discuss apparent deception and apparent self-preservation in chatbots without anthropomorphizing them.
events.uncertain: The November 8 date is the online publication date. The print issue may be dated later in November 2023.

events.title: Nina Beguš, Artificial Humanities
events.description: This study calls for humanistic approaches to AI. It reads fictional and cultural imaginings of artificial beings, from Pygmalion onward, alongside the development of language technologies.
events.uncertain: The publication year, the publisher, and the full subtitle (believed to be A Fictional Perspective on Language in AI) should be verified, and the press URL should be replaced with the book's own page.

events.title: Pascal's calculating machine (the Pascaline)
events.description: The young Pascal designed a geared machine that could add and subtract, to help with his father's tax calculations. It is among the first mechanical calculators to be built and shown in public, and it began a long line of arithmetic machines.
events.uncertain: 1642 is when Pascal began the design. He presented a finished machine in 1645 and received a royal privilege in 1649.

events.title: The Jacquard loom
events.description: Jacquard demonstrated a loom attachment whose woven patterns were controlled by chains of punched cards. Babbage later adopted the punched card as a way to program his Analytical Engine.
events.uncertain: Sources give either 1801 (exhibition) or 1804 (the working mechanism).

events.title: Babbage proposes the Difference Engine
events.description: Babbage announced a plan for a machine that would compute and print mathematical tables using the method of finite differences. The project was never finished, but it led him to design the general-purpose Analytical Engine.
events.uncertain: The proposal was announced in a June 1822 paper to the Astronomical Society. A small demonstration model existed in the same year.

events.title: Ada Lovelace's Notes on the Analytical Engine
events.description: Lovelace translated Menabrea's French account of Babbage's Analytical Engine and added notes much longer than the original article, including a procedure for computing Bernoulli numbers. Her Note G also takes up the question of whether a machine can originate anything, which Turing later called Lady Lovelace's objection.
events.quote: The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate any thing.
events.quote_attribution: Lovelace, Notes by the Translator, Note G (Taylor's Scientific Memoirs, vol. 3, 1843)
events.uncertain: Check the exact spelling 'any thing' against a facsimile of the 1843 text.

events.title: Boole's The Laws of Thought
events.description: Boole set out an algebra of logic in which reasoning about classes and propositions becomes calculation. Boolean algebra later became the basis for digital circuit design.

events.title: Turing's "On Computable Numbers"
events.description: Turing defined an abstract machine that reads and writes symbols on a tape, and used it to show that some mathematical problems cannot be decided by any mechanical procedure. His idea of a universal machine became the theoretical model of the stored-program computer.
events.uncertain: The paper appeared in Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society, ser. 2, vol. 42, which is dated 1936–37.

events.title: McCulloch and Pitts model the neuron as a logic unit
events.description: Their paper treated neurons as simple threshold units and showed that networks of such units could compute logical functions. It is the founding text of artificial neural networks.

events.title: ENIAC unveiled
events.who: J. Presper Eckert, John Mauchly, and team, University of Pennsylvania
events.description: The Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer, built for US Army ballistics work, was shown to the public. Newspapers called it an electronic brain, and the phrase shaped how the public imagined computers.
events.uncertain: The machine was operational in late 1945. The public announcement was in mid-February 1946.

events.title: Shannon's "A Mathematical Theory of Communication"
events.description: Shannon founded information theory and modeled a message as a choice among possibilities sent through a noisy channel. His examples of English generated by statistical approximation are early ancestors of language models.
events.uncertain: Published in two parts in the Bell System Technical Journal, July and October 1948.

events.title: Turing's "Computing Machinery and Intelligence"
events.description: In the journal Mind, Turing replaced the question of whether machines can think with an imitation game played through typed conversation. The test makes dialogue the measure of machine intelligence, and the paper answers objections that include one from Lovelace.

events.title: Georgetown–IBM machine translation demonstration
events.description: An IBM 701 translated more than sixty Russian sentences into English using a small vocabulary and a handful of rules. The publicity encouraged optimistic predictions and government funding for machine translation.

events.title: Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence
events.who: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, Claude Shannon
events.description: The 1955 proposal for this workshop introduced the term artificial intelligence, and the summer meeting gathered the field's founders. It is conventionally treated as the birth of AI as a research discipline.
events.uncertain: The term dates from the 1955 proposal. The workshop itself ran for several weeks in 1956.

events.title: Rosenblatt's perceptron
events.description: Rosenblatt described a neural network that learns to classify inputs by adjusting the weights on its connections. Press coverage promised machines that would walk, talk, and be conscious, an early instance of AI hype.
events.uncertain: The Psychological Review paper is 1958. A Navy press event was held the same year.

events.title: ELIZA
events.description: Weizenbaum's program matched keywords in typed input and returned rearranged replies, most famously in a DOCTOR script that parodied a Rogerian therapist. Users' readiness to confide in it gave its name to the ELIZA effect.
events.uncertain: Written 1964–66 and published in Communications of the ACM, January 1966.

events.title: SHRDLU
events.description: SHRDLU carried on English dialogue about a simulated world of blocks, following commands and answering questions about what it had done and why. It showed how much apparent understanding could come from restricting the world.
events.uncertain: Dated variously 1968–1972. The dissertation is 1971 and the book Understanding Natural Language is 1972.

events.title: PARRY, and PARRY's conversation with ELIZA
events.description: Colby's PARRY simulated a person with paranoid schizophrenia, and in tests psychiatrists had trouble telling its transcripts from those of real patients. In 1972 PARRY was connected to ELIZA over the ARPANET for a conversation between two programs.
events.uncertain: PARRY was developed c. 1971–72. The ELIZA–PARRY session was at ICCC in October 1972, and its transcript was published as RFC 439 in January 1973.

events.title: The Lighthill Report
events.who: James Lighthill, for the UK Science Research Council
events.description: Lighthill's review concluded that AI had not kept its grand promises. It led to deep cuts in British AI funding and is a marker of the first AI winter.

events.title: MYCIN and the expert system
events.description: MYCIN used hundreds of if-then rules from physicians to recommend treatments for bacterial infections, and it could explain its reasoning when asked. It became the model for the rule-based expert systems of the 1980s.
events.uncertain: Shortliffe's dissertation is 1974 and his book Computer-Based Medical Consultations: MYCIN is 1976.

events.title: Backpropagation popularized
events.who: David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, Ronald Williams
events.description: A Nature paper showed that multi-layer neural networks could learn useful internal representations by propagating errors backward through the network. It revived connectionist research.
events.uncertain: The method had earlier precursors, notably Linnainmaa (1970) and Werbos (1974).

events.title: IBM's statistical approach to machine translation
events.description: The IBM group proposed learning translation from aligned parallel texts by probability rather than hand-written grammar rules. The paper marks the statistical turn in natural language processing.
events.uncertain: The 1990 paper is in Computational Linguistics. The fuller 1993 paper is often cited instead.

events.title: First Loebner Prize contest
events.who: Hugh Loebner and the Cambridge Center for Behavioral Studies
events.description: The first annual staged Turing test was held at the Computer Museum in Boston, with judges chatting through terminals. Winning programs often relied on whimsy and evasion, which sharpened debate about what conversation tests measure.

events.title: Deep Blue defeats Kasparov
events.description: IBM's chess computer won the deciding game of a six-game rematch against world champion Garry Kasparov. The match became a cultural symbol of machines surpassing humans at an intellectual game.

events.title: Siri ships on the iPhone 4S
events.description: Apple introduced a voice assistant with a name, a scripted personality, and witty replies to personal questions. It brought the talking assistant persona into everyday consumer use.
events.uncertain: Siri was announced October 4, 2011 and shipped October 14. A standalone Siri app had existed since 2010.

events.title: Word2vec: "Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space"
events.description: The paper introduced fast methods for learning vectors in which words with similar contexts lie close together. The famous analogy arithmetic, king minus man plus woman, made distributional semantics vivid.
events.uncertain: The month is the arXiv v1 date.

events.title: "Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences"
events.who: Paul Christiano et al., OpenAI and DeepMind
events.description: The authors trained agents from human comparisons between pairs of behaviors instead of a hand-written reward. The method became the basis of RLHF for language models.

events.title: "Attention Is All You Need"
events.description: The paper introduced the transformer, an architecture built entirely on attention that processes sequences without recurrence. Nearly every later large language model is built on it.
events.uncertain: Presented at NeurIPS in December 2017.

events.title: BERT
events.description: BERT pre-trained a bidirectional transformer by having it predict masked words, then fine-tuned it for many tasks. It set new records across language understanding benchmarks and made pre-training the standard approach.

events.title: GPT-2 and staged release
events.description: OpenAI announced a language model whose generated prose was fluent enough that the company initially withheld the full model, citing misuse risks. The decision started public debate about releasing text generators.
events.uncertain: The full model was released in November 2019.

events.title: "Language Models are Few-Shot Learners" (GPT-3)
events.description: The paper showed that a 175-billion-parameter model could perform new tasks from a few examples placed in its prompt. Prompting became a kind of writing practice in its own right.

events.title: "Learning to Summarize from Human Feedback"
events.description: The authors trained a reward model on human judgments of summaries and then optimized a language model against it. Its summaries were preferred over the human-written reference summaries, showing that RLHF works for language.

events.title: "LaMDA: Language Models for Dialog Applications"
events.description: Google described a family of models fine-tuned specifically for open-ended dialogue, judged on sensibleness, specificity, safety, and groundedness. Later in 2022 an engineer's claim that LaMDA was sentient made it a public controversy.
events.uncertain: Google first announced LaMDA in May 2021. The sentience controversy was in June 2022.

events.title: "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning"
events.description: The paper showed that prompting a model with worked examples of step-by-step reasoning improves its performance on multi-step problems. Visible reasoning text became part of how models are prompted and presented.

events.title: "Training Language Models to Follow Instructions" (InstructGPT)
events.description: OpenAI fine-tuned GPT-3 on human demonstrations and preference rankings so that it followed instructions helpfully. Labelers preferred the much smaller tuned model to the original, and the recipe led directly to ChatGPT.

events.title: ChatGPT released
events.description: OpenAI released a free chat interface to a model trained to act as a helpful assistant. It quickly reached a mass audience and made the AI assistant persona a global cultural presence.

events.title: Shanahan's "Talking About Large Language Models"
events.description: Shanahan cautioned against loosely attributing belief and knowledge to systems that predict text. He argued for careful philosophical vocabulary when describing language models embedded in dialogue systems.
events.uncertain: Published in Communications of the ACM in 2024.

events.title: "Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback"
events.description: Anthropic trained an assistant to critique and revise its own outputs against a written list of principles, using AI rather than human feedback for harmlessness. It made a written document a direct input in shaping a model's character.

events.title: Claude released
events.description: Anthropic made its assistant Claude publicly available, a model trained with constitutional AI methods. Its name and cultivated character extended the assistant persona as a designed literary figure.
events.uncertain: Claude had earlier limited testing with partners.

events.title: GPT-4 released
events.description: OpenAI released a larger multimodal model that performed near human level on many professional exams. Its technical report disclosed little about how the model was built, which marked a turn toward secrecy in the field.

events.title: "Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior"
events.who: Joon Sung Park et al., Stanford and Google
events.description: The researchers populated a small simulated town with language-model characters that remembered, planned, and talked with one another. One emergent result was a Valentine's party organized among the characters, a kind of machine-made social fiction.

events.title: EU AI Act enters into force
events.description: The first comprehensive AI law entered into force, regulating AI systems by risk level. Among other things, it requires chatbots to disclose that users are talking to a machine, with obligations phased in through 2026 and later.
events.uncertain: Check the transparency rules for chatbots (Article 50) and their application date, which is generally given as August 2026.

events.title: Hephaestus's golden attendants in the Iliad
events.description: In Book 18 of the Iliad, the smith-god Hephaestus is helped by maidens made of gold who can move, think, and speak. They are among the earliest literary images of crafted servants with minds.
events.uncertain: The date of the Homeric poems' composition is disputed; estimates range across the 8th and 7th centuries BCE.

events.title: Talos in the Argonautica
events.description: In Book 4 of the Argonautica, Medea defeats the bronze giant Talos, a guardian of Crete. She does so by draining the single vein that carries his life.
events.uncertain: The poem's exact date is uncertain. The Talos myth is older than Apollonius and appears in earlier sources and vase painting.

events.title: Pygmalion in Ovid's Metamorphoses
events.description: In Book 10 of the Metamorphoses, the sculptor Pygmalion falls in love with an ivory woman he has carved. Venus brings her to life.
events.uncertain: The Metamorphoses is usually dated to about 8 CE, the year of Ovid's exile; its circulation date is approximate.

events.title: Yan Shi's artificial man in the Liezi
events.date_display: c. 4th century CE (approximate compilation of the text)
events.description: A Daoist text tells how the artificer Yan Shi presents King Mu of Zhou with a lifelike performing man built of leather, wood, and lacquer. The king grows angry when the figure flirts with his concubines, and Yan Shi takes it apart to show it is artificial.
events.uncertain: The Liezi is traditionally dated to the 5th century BCE, but most scholars place its compilation around the 4th century CE.

events.title: Rava creates a man (Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b)
events.date_display: c. 500 CE (approximate redaction of the Babylonian Talmud)
events.description: In a brief Talmudic passage, the sage Rava creates a man and sends him to Rabbi Zeira. The figure cannot speak, and Rabbi Zeira returns him to dust; this is a founding text for later golem traditions.
events.uncertain: The Talmud's redaction date is approximate. The famous Prague golem legend associated with Rabbi Loew appears in print only in the 19th century.

events.title: Al-Jazari's Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices
events.description: The engineer al-Jazari described and illustrated water clocks, humanoid servants, and a boat of musical automata in a treatise for the Artuqid court. The work is a landmark in the history of programmable mechanism.

events.title: Legend of Albertus Magnus's talking head
events.date_display: 13th century (period of the legend's subject; recorded later)
events.description: Later medieval and early modern stories claimed that the scholar Albertus Magnus built a speaking head or android. In the legend, his pupil Thomas Aquinas destroyed it.
events.uncertain: This is a legend recorded well after Albertus's lifetime, so no single date applies.

events.title: Vaucanson exhibits the Flute Player
events.description: Vaucanson showed a life-size automaton that played the flute by controlling breath and finger movements. The following year he added the famous Digesting Duck.
events.uncertain: Construction began in 1737; the presentation to the Académie des sciences was in 1738.

events.title: The Mechanical Turk
events.description: Kempelen unveiled a chess-playing automaton dressed as a Turk, which toured Europe and America for decades. It was a hoax worked by a hidden human player.

events.title: Jaquet-Droz's The Writer
events.description: The Swiss watchmaker Pierre Jaquet-Droz built a boy automaton that writes a programmable text of up to about forty characters with a quill. It belongs to a set with a draughtsman and a musician that survives in Neuchâtel.
events.uncertain: Dates of 1768 to 1774 are given for the set of three automata.

events.title: "The Sandman"
events.description: The student Nathanael falls in love with Olimpia, who turns out to be an automaton, and he descends into madness. Freud later made the story central to his essay on the uncanny.
events.uncertain: The first volume of Nachtstücke appeared in late 1816 with an 1817 imprint.

events.title: "Maelzel's Chess-Player"
events.date_display: April 1836 (publication in the Southern Literary Messenger)
events.description: Poe published an essay arguing that the touring chess automaton must be operated by a concealed human. He reasoned from the machine's behavior to the necessity of a mind inside it.

events.title: "The Artist of the Beautiful"
events.description: A watchmaker spends years building a delicate mechanical butterfly that seems alive. When it is crushed, the story turns the loss into a meditation on art and spirit.
events.uncertain: First published in the Democratic Review in 1844; collected in Mosses from an Old Manse (1846).

events.title: Erewhon ("The Book of the Machines")
events.description: In Butler's satirical utopia, the Erewhonians have destroyed their machines for fear that machines would evolve consciousness. The chapters on machines grew from his 1863 letter "Darwin among the Machines."
events.uncertain: The novel was published anonymously.

events.title: Tomorrow's Eve (L'Ève future)
events.description: A fictionalized Thomas Edison builds Hadaly, an artificial woman whose speech comes from phonograph recordings, for a disappointed English lord. The novel popularized the word android.
events.uncertain: Parts of the novel were serialized in 1885 to 1886 before the book edition.

events.title: "Moxon's Master"
events.description: An inventor who argues that machines can think is killed by his chess-playing automaton after he beats it. The story is an early American tale of a machine's resentment.
events.uncertain: First printed in the San Francisco Examiner in 1899; collected in 1909. Confirm the exact newspaper date.

events.title: Tik-Tok in Ozma of Oz
events.description: Dorothy finds Tik-Tok, a wind-up copper man whose thinking, speech, and action must each be wound separately. He is one of the first robot-like figures in children's literature.

events.title: "The Machine Stops"
events.date_display: November 1909 (publication in the Oxford and Cambridge Review)
events.description: Humanity lives underground in separate cells and communicates only through a global Machine that meets every need, until the Machine breaks down. The story anticipates networked, mediated conversation.

events.title: Metropolis
events.description: In a stratified future city, the inventor Rotwang builds a robot in the likeness of the worker-saint Maria to incite revolt. The robot's transformation scene became a defining image of the machine woman.
events.uncertain: The film entered the US public domain in 2023; restored versions may carry separate rights. Von Harbou's novel appeared in 1925 to 1926.

events.title: "Runaround" and the Three Laws of Robotics
events.description: This story is the first to state Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics explicitly. In it, a robot on Mercury is caught in a loop between conflicting laws.

events.title: I, Robot
events.description: Asimov collected his robot stories from the 1940s in a frame narrative told by the robopsychologist Susan Calvin. The collection made the rule-bound, reasoning robot a standard figure.

events.title: Forbidden Planet
events.description: A loose science-fiction version of The Tempest features Robby the Robot, a polite, multilingual mechanical servant. The film also involves a monster made by an alien machine from the id.
events.uncertain: Confirm the exact March 1956 release date.

events.title: The Cyberiad
events.description: Comic fables follow two robot constructors, Trurl and Klapaucius, in a universe of machines. One tale features the Electronic Bard, a poetry-writing machine.
events.uncertain: Michael Kandel's English translation appeared in 1974.

events.title: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
events.description: A bounty hunter in a ruined San Francisco tracks escaped androids using an empathy test given in conversation. The novel asks whether empathy marks the human.

events.title: 2001: A Space Odyssey
events.description: The ship's computer HAL 9000 talks with the crew in a calm, courteous voice and then turns against them. HAL became the archetype of the conversational machine whose politeness hides its aims.
events.uncertain: Clarke's novel was published later in 1968.

events.title: Blade Runner
events.description: This loose adaptation of Dick's novel follows Deckard as he hunts replicants who are trying to extend their four-year lives. The Voight-Kampff interview stages the boundary between human and machine as a conversation.

events.title: Neuromancer
events.description: A burned-out hacker is hired for a job that turns out to serve Wintermute, an AI seeking to merge with its counterpart. The novel defined cyberpunk and popularized the term cyberspace.

events.title: He, She and It
events.description: In a future Jewish free town, the cyborg Yod is built as a protector, and his story is braided with a retelling of the Prague golem. The novel joins golem legend with cyberpunk.
events.uncertain: Published in the UK as Body of Glass.

events.title: Galatea 2.2
events.description: A novelist named Richard Powers helps train a neural network to pass a master's exam in English literature. The novel is a modern Pygmalion about teaching a machine to read.

events.title: A.I. Artificial Intelligence
events.who: Steven Spielberg (director), from a project developed by Stanley Kubrick
events.description: David, a child android programmed to love, is abandoned and searches for the Blue Fairy to become a real boy. The film draws on Brian Aldiss's story "Supertoys Last All Summer Long" and on Pinocchio.

events.title: The Lifecycle of Software Objects
events.description: Former zookeepers spend years raising digital creatures called digients, which learn language through long care and teaching. The novella treats AI development as upbringing.

events.title: Her
events.description: A lonely letter writer falls in love with Samantha, a conversational operating system known only as a voice. The film imagines intimacy with an AI as pure dialogue.
events.uncertain: General US release followed in December 2013 and January 2014.

events.title: Ex Machina
events.description: A programmer is invited to give a Turing-style test to Ava, a humanoid AI, in a series of interview sessions. Ava turns the test into an instrument of escape.
events.uncertain: There was a December 2014 screening in London before the UK release.

events.title: Machines Like Me
events.description: In an alternative 1980s London where Turing lived, a man buys Adam, one of the first synthetic humans, who writes haiku and holds rigid moral views. The novel treats the android as a lodger and a rival in love.

events.title: Klara and the Sun
events.description: Klara, an Artificial Friend bought as a companion for a sick girl, narrates the family's life through her careful and partial observations. The novel is told from inside the perspective of an attentive, devoted machine.

events.title: Plato, Meno
events.description: Socrates questions an enslaved boy about a geometry problem and leads him toward a solution, a scene that becomes a model of teaching by question rather than by telling. The dialogue also asks whether virtue can be taught and introduces the idea that learning is recollection.
events.uncertain: Composition date is an estimate. Scholars place it in Plato's early-middle period, roughly 387 to 380 BCE.

events.title: Plato, Symposium
events.description: A series of speeches on love given at a drinking party is reported at second and third hand. The frame and the embedded speeches make it a study of how conversation is remembered, retold, and staged.
events.uncertain: Composition date is an estimate, usually placed between about 385 and 370 BCE.

events.title: Xenophon, Memorabilia
events.description: Xenophon collects conversations he attributes to Socrates in order to defend his teacher's memory. It offers a second, more practical portrait of Socratic conversation that can be set beside Plato's.
events.uncertain: Composition date is uncertain. It was probably written in stages after 371 BCE.

events.title: Cicero, On the Orator (De Oratore)
events.description: Cicero sets out his theory of eloquence as a conversation among leading Roman orators at a country villa. The work brings the Platonic dialogue form into Latin rhetoric and the education of public speakers.
events.uncertain: This is the date of composition.

events.title: Lucian, Dialogues of the Dead
events.description: In short comic exchanges, the shades of the dead in the underworld mock wealth, fame, and philosophical pretension. Lucian turns the philosophical dialogue into satire and founds a genre that many later writers imitated.
events.uncertain: The composition date is only approximate (mid-second century CE).

events.title: Augustine, Soliloquies
events.description: Augustine writes a dialogue between himself and a personified Reason about God and the soul. The work is an early example of dialogue turned inward, with the self split into two speakers.
events.uncertain: These are the dates of composition, at Cassiciacum before his baptism.

events.title: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy
events.description: While imprisoned and awaiting execution, Boethius writes a dialogue in prose and verse in which Lady Philosophy appears and counsels him. It became one of the most widely read and translated books of the Middle Ages.
events.uncertain: This is the date of composition. It falls between 523 and 525.

events.title: Baldassare Castiglione, The Book of the Courtier
events.description: Courtiers at Urbino spend several evenings in conversation describing the ideal courtier, including the art of seeming effortless. The book treats polished conversation as a social performance and shaped European manners for centuries.
events.uncertain: This is the date of first publication (Venice, Aldine Press). It was composed over many years from about 1508.

events.title: Galileo Galilei, Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems
events.description: Three speakers debate the Copernican and Ptolemaic systems over four days, and the Aristotelian Simplicio is often made to look foolish. The book led to Galileo's trial by the Inquisition in 1633.
events.uncertain: This is the date of first publication (Florence, February 1632).

events.title: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion
events.description: Three characters argue over whether the order of nature proves the existence of a designer. Hume never makes clear which speaker voices his own view, which makes the book a classic case of arguing through several characters.
events.uncertain: This is the date of posthumous first publication. Hume wrote and revised it from the 1750s until his death in 1776.

events.title: Denis Diderot, Rameau's Nephew
events.who: Denis Diderot; translated by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
events.description: A philosopher and the parasitic, brilliant nephew of the composer Rameau talk in a Paris café, and the nephew mimics and performs whole roles. The work was unpublished in Diderot's lifetime and first appeared in Goethe's German translation.
events.uncertain: It was composed about 1761 to 1774. The French text first appeared in 1821 (a retranslation from German) and in authentic form in 1891.

events.title: Martin Buber, I and Thou
events.description: Buber distinguishes the relation of mutual address between I and You from the relation of I to It, in which the other is used or observed as an object. The book became a founding text of the philosophy of dialogue.
events.uncertain: This is the date of the German first edition (Ich und Du). The English translation appeared in 1937. US public-domain status applies to the 1923 German text.

events.title: Mikhail Bakhtin, Problems of Dostoevsky's Art
events.description: Bakhtin argues that Dostoevsky's novels are polyphonic: many independent voices sound in them without being merged into the author's single view. The book lays the groundwork for his theory of dialogism.
events.uncertain: This is the date of the first Russian edition. A much revised version appeared in 1963 as Problems of Dostoevsky's Poetics. English translations date from 1973 and 1984 and are in copyright.

events.title: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations
events.description: Wittgenstein's posthumous book argues that meaning lies in use within language games and forms of life. It proceeds through questions, objections, and replies from imagined interlocutors.
events.uncertain: This is the date of posthumous publication. It was composed mainly from 1936 to 1949.

events.title: J. L. Austin, How to Do Things with Words
events.description: Austin shows that many utterances, such as promises and verdicts, perform actions rather than describe the world. The book founded speech act theory.
events.uncertain: This is the date of posthumous publication. The text derives from the 1955 William James Lectures at Harvard.

events.title: Erving Goffman, Interaction Ritual
events.description: Goffman's essays analyze face-to-face encounters as rituals in which people protect their own face and the face of others. His concept of face-work later shaped the study of politeness.
events.uncertain: This is the book's date. Its key essay, On Face-Work, first appeared in 1955.

events.title: John Searle, Speech Acts
events.description: Searle systematizes Austin's ideas into rules for acts such as promising and asserting. He treats speaking a language as a form of rule-governed behavior.

events.title: Joseph Weizenbaum, Computer Power and Human Reason
events.description: The creator of ELIZA describes his alarm that people confided in his simple program as though it understood them. He argues that some tasks, such as judgment and care, should not be handed to computers.

events.title: Schegloff, Jefferson, and Sacks, The Preference for Self-Correction in the Organization of Repair in Conversation
events.who: Emanuel Schegloff, Gail Jefferson, Harvey Sacks
events.description: This companion to the turn-taking paper shows how speakers fix troubles in speaking, hearing, and understanding. It finds that conversation is organized so that speakers tend to correct themselves.
events.uncertain: Published in Language 53(2). The source page is a general article on repair rather than the paper itself.

events.title: Brown and Levinson, politeness theory
events.who: Penelope Brown and Stephen C. Levinson
events.description: Building on Goffman's idea of face, Brown and Levinson propose universal strategies speakers use to soften acts that threaten face. Their model became central to the study of politeness and indirect speech.
events.uncertain: First published as a long essay in Questions and Politeness (ed. Goody, 1978). It was reissued as the book Politeness in 1987.

events.title: Michael Reddy, The Conduit Metaphor
events.description: Reddy shows that English speakers habitually describe communication as packing meanings into words and sending them to a listener. He argues that this metaphor hides the active work listeners do to reconstruct meaning.
events.uncertain: Published in Metaphor and Thought, edited by Andrew Ortony.

events.title: John Searle, Minds, Brains, and Programs (the Chinese Room)
events.description: Searle imagines a person who follows rules for manipulating Chinese symbols and produces fluent answers without understanding Chinese. He argues that running a program is not enough for understanding.
events.uncertain: Published in Behavioral and Brain Sciences 3(3), with peer commentaries.

events.title: Clark and Brennan, Grounding in Communication
events.who: Herbert H. Clark and Susan E. Brennan
events.description: Clark and Brennan describe how conversational partners work together to establish that they have understood each other well enough. They show how the medium of communication changes the cost of this grounding.
events.uncertain: Published in Perspectives on Socially Shared Cognition (APA, 1991).

events.title: Bender and Koller, Climbing towards NLU (the octopus test)
events.who: Emily M. Bender and Alexander Koller
events.description: Using the thought experiment of an octopus that eavesdrops on an undersea cable, the authors argue that a system trained only on linguistic form cannot learn meaning. The paper revived Chinese Room-style debates for large language models.
events.uncertain: Presented at ACL 2020, held online in July 2020.
